title: Rajkummar Rao Prosecutes the Man Who Attacked Mumbai. Prahaar Might Be the Most Important Courtroom Drama Bollywood Has Ever Attempted.
excerpt: Maddock Films bets on the 26/11 Kasab trial with the director of Paatal Lok, a career-best cast, and a story that still makes the diaspora's blood run cold.
body:
On the night of November 26, 2008, ten men armed with assault rifles and grenades entered Mumbai by sea and attacked the city for 60 hours. 166 people died. One attacker survived. His name was **Ajmal Kasab**, and the man who prosecuted him — who built the case that led to his conviction and eventual execution — was **Ujjwal Nikam**, a special public prosecutor who had already spent decades in some of India's most explosive courtrooms.

Now **Rajkummar Rao** is playing him. And the film is called **Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story**.

## The Prosecutor Who Became a Legend

**Ujjwal Nikam** is not your typical biopic subject. He's not a freedom fighter, a sports star, or a politician. He's a lawyer — but a lawyer who prosecuted the 1993 Bombay bombings case, the Gulshan Kumar murder trial, the Pramod Mahajan murder case, and, most famously, the 26/11 Mumbai attacks trial. He became a household name in India not for glamour but for a kind of relentless, furious precision in the courtroom. When you're prosecuting a man caught alive after killing 52 people at CST station, there is no room for theatrics. Only evidence, argument, and an absolute refusal to lose.

The film, directed by **Avinash Arun** — the man behind the critically acclaimed *Three of Us* and the first season of *Paatal Lok* — won't attempt to cover Nikam's entire career. Instead, Maddock Films has confirmed it will zero in on the Kasab trial specifically: the intense legal and moral battle that followed the worst terrorist attack on Indian soil.

## Rajkummar Rao Builds His Case

**Rajkummar Rao** has been the quiet workhorse of Hindi cinema for a decade. While bigger names chased franchise tentpoles, he built a filmography that includes *Newton*, *Bareilly Ki Barfi*, *Trapped*, *Shahid*, and the *Stree* series. His collaboration with **Dinesh Vijan**'s Maddock Films — this will be their sixth project together — has become one of Bollywood's most productive creative partnerships.

But *Prahaar* asks something different. This is not comedy. This is not genre play. This is courtroom drama rooted in one of the most traumatic events in modern Indian history. Rao will need to channel the controlled fury and intellectual intensity of a man who sat across from a terrorist and methodically dismantled every possible defence.

The supporting cast is stacked. **Jaideep Ahlawat**, who has evolved into one of Indian cinema's most commanding screen presences since *Paatal Lok* and *An Action Hero*, takes a pivotal role — though the exact character hasn't been revealed. **Wamiqa Gabbi**, fresh off *Bhool Chuk Maaf* and the Netflix hit *Bhooth Bangla*, reunites with Rao. **Sikandar Kher** completes the ensemble.

> "Rarely does a producer have two prominent releases in the same month, but Dinesh Vijan is set to achieve just that in August 2026." — **Taran Adarsh**, trade analyst

## The Avinash Arun Factor

This is the detail that should excite anyone who cares about filmmaking craft. **Avinash Arun** is not a mainstream Bollywood director — he's a cinematographer-turned-director whose work in *Paatal Lok* redefined what Indian streaming could look like visually. His feature *Three of Us*, starring Shefali Shah, was a quiet, devastating film about memory and loss that played festivals worldwide.

Handing him a courtroom drama about the Kasab trial is an inspired choice. Expect visual restraint, emotional intensity, and the kind of slow-building dread that made *Paatal Lok* so unforgettable. This won't be a Bollywood courtroom scene with dramatic music cues and standing ovations. It'll be closer to *A Few Good Men* — if *A Few Good Men* was about the worst night in Mumbai's history.

## Why This Matters for NRI Audiences

26/11 is personal for the Indian diaspora. Many NRIs watched the attacks unfold in real time on television, thousands of miles away, unable to do anything. The trial that followed — and the eventual execution of Kasab in 2012 — was a moment of catharsis for millions. Nikam became a symbol of the Indian justice system at its most determined.

For the diaspora, *Prahaar* is not just a film about a prosecutor. It's a film about whether justice can answer violence, whether a courtroom can heal a city, and whether one man's relentless pursuit of conviction can stand in for an entire nation's grief.

*Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story* opens in theatres worldwide on **August 7, 2026**.
